I.def.1: A point A is that which has no part.
I.def.2: A line [ A B ] is a projection of a relationship of two points A, B.
I.def.3: The extremities of a segment / A B / are points A, B.
I.def.4: A segment / A B / is a portion of a line [ A B ] between two points A, B on the line.
I.def.5: A surface is that which has length and breadth only.
I.def.6: The extremities of a surface are lines or arcs.
I.def.7: A plane surface lies evenly with the lines on itself.
I.def.8: A plane angle is the inclination to one another of two lines or arcs in a plane that meet and do not lie on the same line.
I.def.9: A rectilineal angle is contained by two segments or lines.
I.def.10: When a segment standing on a line makes the adjacent angles equal, each of the equal angles is a right angle, and the standing segment is perpendicular to the line.
I.def.11: An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle.
I.def.12: An acute angle is less than a right angle.
I.def.13: A boundary is the extremity of anything.
I.def.14: A figure is that which is contained by any boundary or boundaries.
I.def.15: A circle ( A B ) is a plane figure contained by one arc defined by a center A and a point B establishing its defining radius / A B /, such that all segments / A B /, / A C /, / A D / falling upon the arc from A are equal.
I.def.16: The point A within the circle ( A B ) from which all segments / A B /, / A C / to the arc are equal is called the center of the circle.
I.def.17: A diameter of a circle is any segment drawn through the center and terminated in both directions by the arc of the circle; it bisects the circle.
I.def.18: A semicircle is the figure contained by a diameter and the arc cut off by it.
I.def.19: Rectilineal figures are contained by segments: trilateral by three, quadrilateral by four, and multilateral by more than four.
I.def.20: Of trilateral figures, an equilateral triangle < A B C > has three equal sides, an isosceles triangle < D E F > has two equal sides, and a scalene triangle < G H K > has three unequal sides.
I.def.21: A right-angled triangle has a right angle, an obtuse-angled triangle has an obtuse angle, and an acute-angled triangle has three acute angles.
I.def.22: Of quadrilateral figures, a square is equilateral and right-angled; an oblong is right-angled but not equilateral; a rhombus is equilateral but not right-angled; a rhomboid has opposite sides and angles equal but is neither equilateral nor right-angled.
I.def.23: Parallel lines are lines in the same plane which, extended indefinitely in both directions, do not meet.
I.post.1: Construct a segment / A B / between any two points A, B.
I.post.2: Extend a segment / A B / continuously along a line [ A B ] to / B C /.
I.post.3: Construct a circle ( A B ) with center A and defining radius point B.
I.post.5: Two lines intersected by a transversal with interior angles on one side summing to less than two right angles meet on that side.
I.cn.1: Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
I.cn.2: If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
I.cn.3: If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.
I.cn.4: Things / A B /, / D E / that coincide with one another are equal to one another.
I.cn.5: The whole is greater than the part.
I.1: Construct an equilateral triangle on a given segment.
I.2: Construct at a given point a segment equal to a given segment.
I.3: Cut off from the greater of two unequal segments a segment equal to the less.
I.4: Triangles with two sides and the included angle equal are congruent (SAS).
I.5: In an isosceles triangle, the angles at the base are equal, and if the equal sides are extended, the angles under the base are equal.
I.6: If two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides subtending the equal angles are also equal.
I.7: On the same segment and on the same side, there cannot be constructed two distinct triangles with both pairs of conterminous sides equal.
I.8: Triangles with all three corresponding sides equal have their corresponding angles equal (SSS).
I.11: Construct a segment at right angles to a given line from a given point on it.
I.12: Construct a perpendicular to a given line from a given point not on it.
I.13: A segment standing on a line makes either two right angles or adjacent angles summing to two right angles.
I.14: If two segments at a point on a line on opposite sides make adjacent angles summing to two right angles, the two segments are collinear.
I.15: Intersecting lines make their vertical angles equal.
I.16: In any triangle, if one side is extended, the exterior angle is greater than either opposite interior angle.
I.17: In any triangle, the sum of any two angles is less than two right angles.
I.18: In any triangle, the greater side subtends the greater angle.
I.19: In any triangle, the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.
I.20: In any triangle, the sum of any two sides is greater than the remaining side.
I.21: Segments constructed from the endpoints of one side of a triangle to an interior point have a lesser sum but contain a greater angle than the other two sides.
I.22: Construct a triangle from three segments equal to three given segments satisfying the triangle inequality.
I.23: Construct on a given line at a given point an angle equal to a given angle.
I.24: If two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively, the one with the greater included angle has the greater base.
I.25: If two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively, the one with the greater base has the greater included angle.
I.26: Triangles with two angles and one corresponding side equal are congruent (ASA / AAS).
I.27: If a transversal cutting two lines makes the alternate interior angles equal, the lines are parallel.
I.28: If a transversal cutting two lines makes the exterior angle equal to the opposite interior angle, or interior angles on the same side supplementary, the lines are parallel.
I.29: A transversal cutting parallel lines makes alternate interior angles equal, exterior and opposite interior angles equal, and same-side interior angles supplementary.
I.30: Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to one another.
I.31: Construct through a given point a line parallel to a given line.
I.32: In any triangle, an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, and the three interior angles sum to two right angles.
I.33: Segments joining the endpoints of equal and parallel segments in the same directions are themselves equal and parallel.
I.34: In a parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, and the diagonal bisects the area.
I.35: Parallelograms on the same base and in the same parallels are equal in area.
I.36: Parallelograms on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal in area.
I.37: Triangles on the same base and in the same parallels are equal in area.
I.38: Triangles on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal in area.
I.39: Equal triangles on the same base and on the same side lie in the same parallels.
I.40: Equal triangles on equal bases and on the same side lie in the same parallels.
I.41: If a parallelogram shares the same base with a triangle and lies in the same parallels, the parallelogram is double the triangle.
I.42: Construct, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given triangle.
I.43: In any parallelogram, the complements of the parallelograms about the diagonal are equal in area.
I.44: Apply to a given segment, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given triangle.
I.45: Construct, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given polygon.
I.46: Construct a square on a given segment.
I.47: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the two legs (Pythagorean Theorem).
I.48: If the square on one side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, the angle contained by those two sides is right.
II.def.1: Any rectangular parallelogram is said to becontained by the twosegments containing theright angle.
II.def.2: And in any parallelogrammic area let any one whatever of the parallelograms about itsdiameter with the two complements be called agnomon.
II.1: If there be two segments, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two segments is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut segment and each of the segments.
II.2: If a segment be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole.
II.3: If a segment be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment.
II.4: If a segment be cut at random, the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments.
II.5: If a segment be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the segment between the points of section is equal to the square on the half.
II.6: If a segment be bisected and a segment be added to it in a segment, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added segment and the added segment together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the segment made up of the half and the added segment.
II.7: If a segment be cut at random, the square on the whole and that on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment and the square on the remaining segment.
II.8: If a segment be cut at random, four times the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments together with the square on the remaining segment is equal to the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one segment.
II.9: If a segment be cut into equal and unequal segments, the squares on the unequal segments of the whole are double of the square on the half and of the square on the segment between the points of section.
II.10: If a segment be bisected, and a segment be added to it in a segment, the square on the whole with the added segment and the square on the added segment both together are double of the square on the half and of the square described on the segment made up of the half and the added segment as on one segment.
II.11: Cut a given segment so that the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the square on the remaining segment.
II.12: In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the segment cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.
II.13: In acute-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the acute angle is less than the squares on the sides containing the acute angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the acute angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the segment cut off within by the perpendicular towards the acute angle.
II.14: Construct a square equal to a given polygon.
III.def.1: Equal circles are those thediameters of which are equal, or the radii of which are equal.
III.def.2: Asegment is said totouch a circle which, meeting thecircle and being produced, does not cut the circle.
III.def.3: Circles are said totouch one another which, meeting one another, do not cut one another.
III.def.4: In acirclesegments are said to beequally distant from the center when theperpendiculars drawn to them from thecenter are equal.
III.def.5: And thatsegment is said to beat a greater distance on which the greaterperpendicular falls.
III.def.6: Asegment of a circle is thefigure contained by asegment and a arc of acircle.
III.def.7: Anangle of a segment is that contained by asegment and a arc of acircle.
III.def.8: Anangle in a segment is theangle which, when apoint is taken on the arc of the segment andsegments are joined from it to theextremities of the segment which is thebase of the segment, is contained by the segments so joined.
III.def.9: And, when thesegments containing theangle cut off a arc, the angle is said tostand upon that arc.
III.def.10: Asector of a circle is thefigure which, when anangle is constructed at thecenter of thecircle, is contained by thesegments containing the angle and the arc cut off by them.
III.def.11: Similar segments of circles are those which admit equalangles, or in which the angles are equal.
III.1: Find the center of a given circle.
III.2: If on the arc of a circle two points be taken at random, the segment joining the points will fall within the circle.
III.3: If in a circle a segment through the center bisect a segment not through the center, it also cuts it at right angles; and if it cut it at right angles, it also bisects it.
III.4: If in a circle two segments cut one another which are not through the center, they do not bisect one another.
III.5: If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same center.
III.6: If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same center.
III.7: If on the diameter of a circle a point be taken which is not the center of the circle, and from the point segments fall upon the circle, that is greatest on which the center is, the remainder of the same diameter is least, and of the rest the nearer to the segment through the center is always greater than the more remote, and only two equal segments will fall from the point on the circle, one on each side of the least segment.
III.8: If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point segments be drawn through to the circle, one of which is through the center and the others are drawn at random, then, of the segments which fall on the concave arc, that through the center is greatest, while of the rest the nearer to that through the center is always greater than the more remote, but, of the segments falling on the convex arc, that between the point and the diameter is least, while of the rest the nearer to the least is always less than the more remote, and only two equal segments will fall on the circle from the point, one on each side of the least.
III.9: If a point be taken within a circle, and more than two equal segments fall from the point on the circle, the point taken is the center of the circle.
III.10: A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.
III.11: If two circles touch one another internally, and their centres be taken, the segment joining their centres, if it be also produced, will fall on the point of contact of the circles.
III.12: If two circles touch one another externally, the segment joining their centres will pass through the point of contact.
III.13: A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally.
III.14: In a circle equal segments are equally distant from the center, and those which are equally distant from the center are equal.
III.15: Of segments in a circle the diameter is greatest, and of the rest the nearer to the center is always greater than the more remote.
III.16: The segment drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity will fall outside the circle, and into the space between the segment and the arc another segment cannot be interposed; further the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute angle.
III.17: From a given point to draw a segment touching a given circle.
III.18: If a segment touch a circle, and a segment be joined from the center to the point of contact, the segment so joined is perpendicular to the tangent.
III.19: If a segment touch a circle, and from the point of contact a segment be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the center of the circle is on the segment so drawn.
III.20: In a circle the angle at the center is double of the angle at the arc, when the angles have the same arc as base.
III.21: In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal.
III.22: The opposite angles of quadrilaterals in circles are equal to two right angles.
III.23: On the same segment there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles on the same side.
III.24: Similar segments of circles on equal segments are equal.
III.25: Given a segment of a circle, to describe the complete circle of which it is a segment.
III.26: In equal circles equal angles stand on equal arcs, whether they stand at the centres or at the arcs.
III.27: In equal circles angles standing on equal arcs are equal, whether they stand at the centres or at the arcs.
III.28: In equal circles equal segments cut off equal arcs, the greater equal to the greater and the less to the less.
III.29: In equal circles equal arcs are subtended by equal segments.
III.31: In a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, and the angle of the less segment less than a right angle.
III.32: If a segment touch a circle, and from the point of contact there be drawn across, in the circle, a segment cutting the circle, the angles which it makes with the tangent will equals the angles in the alternate segments of the circle.
III.33: Describe on a given segment a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given angle.
III.34: From a given circle to cut off a segment admitting an angle equal to a given angle.
III.35: If in a circle two segments cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.
III.36: If a point be taken outside a circle and from it there fall on the circle two segments, and if one of them cut the circle and the other touch it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the segment which cuts the circle and the segment intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex arc will equals the square on the tangent.
III.37: If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point there fall on the circle two segments, if one of them cut the circle, and the other fall on it, and if further the rectangle contained by the whole of the segment which cuts the circle and the segment intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex arc equals the square on the segment which falls on the circle, the segment which falls on it will touch the circle.
IV.def.1: Apolygon is said to beinscribed in a polygon when the respectiveangles of the inscribedfigure lie on the respective sides of that in which it is inscribed.
IV.def.2: Similarly afigure is said to becircumscribed about a figure when the respective sides of the circumscribed figure pass through the respectiveangles of that about which it is circumscribed.
IV.def.3: Apolygon is said to beinscribed in a circle when eachangle of the inscribedfigure lies on the arc of thecircle.
IV.def.4: Apolygon is said to becircumscribed about a circle, when each side of the circumscribedfigure touches the arc of thecircle.
IV.def.5: Similarly acircle is said to beinscribed in a figure when the arc of the circle touches each side of thefigure in which it is inscribed.
IV.def.6: Acircle is said to becircumscribed about a figure when the arc of the circle passes through eachangle of thefigure about which it is circumscribed.
IV.def.7: Asegment is said to befitted into a circle when itsextremities are on the arc of thecircle.

V.def.1: A magnitude is apart of a magnitude, the less of the greater, when it measures the greater.
V.def.2: The greater is amultiple of the less when it ismeasured by the less.
V.def.3: Aratio is a sort of relation in respect of size between two magnitudes of the same kind.
V.def.4: Magnitudes are said tohave a ratio to one another which are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another.
V.def.5: Magnitudes are said tobe in the same ratio, the first to the second and the third to the fourth, when, if anyequimultiples whatever be taken of the first and third, and any equimultiples whatever of the second and fourth, the former equimultiples alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of, the latter equimultiples respectively taken in corresponding order.
V.def.6: Let magnitudes which have thesame ratio be calledproportional.
V.def.7: When, of theequimultiples, the multiple of the first magnitude exceeds the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth, then the first is said tohave a greater ratio to the second than the third has to the fourth.
V.def.8: A proportion in three terms is the least possible.
V.def.9: When three magnitudes areproportional, the first is said to have to the third theduplicate ratio of that which it has to the second.
V.def.10: When four magnitudes are < continuously >proportional, the first is said to have to the fourth thetriplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and so on continually, whatever be the proportion.
V.def.11: The termcorresponding magnitudes is used of antecedents in relation to antecedents, and of consequents in relation to consequents.
V.def.12: Alternate ratio means taking theantecedent in relation to the antecedent and the consequent in relation to the consequent.
V.def.13: Inverse ratio means taking theconsequent as antecedent in relation to the antecedent as consequent.
V.def.14: Composition of a ratio means taking theantecedent together with the consequent as one in relation to the consequent by itself.
V.def.15: Separation of a ratio means taking the excess by which theantecedent exceeds the consequent in relation to the consequent by itself.
V.def.16: Conversion of a ratio means taking theantecedent in relation to the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent.
V.def.17: Aratioex aequali arises when, there being several magnitudes and another set equal to them in multitude which taken two and two are in the same proportion, as the first is to the last among the first magnitudes, so is the first to the last among the second magnitudes; Or, in other words, it means taking the extreme terms by virtue of the removal of the intermediate terms.
V.def.18: Aperturbed proportion arises when, there being three magnitudes and another set equal to them in multitude, asantecedent is to consequent among the first magnitudes, so is antecedent to consequent among the second magnitudes, while, as the consequent is to a third among the first magnitudes, so is a third to the antecedent among the second magnitudes.
V.1: If there be any number of magnitudes whatever which are, respectively, equimultiples of any magnitudes equal in multitude, then, whatever multiple one of the magnitudes is of one, that multiple also will all be of all.
V.2: If a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and a fifth also be the same multiple of the second that a sixth is of the fourth, the sum of the first and fifth is the same multiple of the second that the sum of the third and sixth is of the fourth.
V.3: If a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and if equimultiples be taken of the first and third, then also ex aequali the magnitudes taken is equimultiples respectively, the one of the second and the other of the fourth.
V.4: If a first magnitude have to a second the same ratio as a third to a fourth, any equimultiples whatever of the first and third will also have the same ratio to any equimultiples whatever of the second and fourth respectively, taken in corresponding order.
V.5: If a magnitude be the same multiple of a magnitude that a part subtracted is of a part subtracted, the remainder is the same multiple of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.
V.6: If two magnitudes be equimultiples of two magnitudes, and any magnitudes subtracted from them be equimultiples of the same, the remainders also are either equal to the same or equimultiples of them.
V.7: Equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio, as also has the same to equal magnitudes.
V.8: Of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has; and the same has to the less a greater ratio than it has to the greater.
V.9: Magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal; and magnitudes to which the same has the same ratio are equal.
V.10: Of magnitudes which have a ratio to the same, that which has a greater ratio is greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less.
V.11: Ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another.
V.12: If any number of magnitudes be proportional, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so will all the antecedents be to all the consequents.
V.13: If a first magnitude have to a second the same ratio as a third to a fourth, and the third have to the fourth a greater ratio than a fifth has to a sixth, the first will also have to the second a greater ratio than the fifth to the sixth.
V.14: If a first magnitude have to a second the same ratio as a third has to a fourth, and the first be greater than the third, the second is greater than the fourth; if equal, equal; and if less, less.
V.15: Parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them taken in corresponding order.
V.16: If four magnitudes be proportional, they is proportional alternately.
V.17: If magnitudes be proportional componendo, they is proportional separando.
V.18: If magnitudes be proportional separando, they is proportional componendo.
V.19: If, as a whole is to a whole, so is a part subtracted to a part subtracted, the remainder is to the remainder as whole to whole.
V.20: If there be three magnitudes, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio, and if ex aequali the first be greater than the third, the fourth is greater than the sixth; if equal, equal; and, if less, less.
V.21: If there be three magnitudes, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two together are in the same ratio, and the proportion of them be perturbed, then, if ex aequali the first magnitude is greater than the third, the fourth is greater than the sixth; if equal, equal; and if less, less.
V.22: If there be any number of magnitudes whatever, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two together are in the same ratio, they is in the same ratio ex aequali.
V.23: If there be three magnitudes, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two together are in the same ratio, and the proportion of them be perturbed, they is in the same ratio ex aequali.
V.24: If a first magnitude have to a second the same ratio as a third has to a fourth, and also a fifth have to the second the same ratio as a sixth to the fourth, the first and fifth added together will have to the second the same ratio as the third and sixth have to the fourth.
V.25: If four magnitudes be proportional, the greatest and the least are greater than the remaining two.
VI.def.1: Similar polygons are such as have theirangles severally equal and the sides about the equal anglesproportional.
VI.def.2: Reciprocally related figures have their sides about equal angles reciprocally proportional.
VI.def.3: A segment is said to have been cut in extreme and mean ratio when, as the wholeline is to the greater segment, so is the greater to the less.
VI.def.4: The height of anyfigure is theperpendicular drawn from the vertex to the base.
VI.1: Triangles and parallelograms which are under the same height are to one another as their bases.
VI.2: If a segment be drawn parallel to one of the sides of a triangle, it will cut the sides of the triangle proportionally; and, if the sides of the triangle be cut proportionally, the line joining the points of section is parallel to the remaining side of the triangle.
VI.3: If an angle of a triangle be bisected and the segment cutting the angle cut the base also, the segments of the base will have the same ratio as the remaining sides of the triangle; and, if the segments of the base have the same ratio as the remaining sides of the triangle, the segment joined from the vertex to the point of section will bisect the angle of the triangle.
VI.4: In equiangular triangles the sides about the equal angles are proportional, and those are corresponding sides which subtend the equal angles.
VI.5: If two triangles have their sides proportional, the triangles is equiangular and will have those angles equal which the corresponding sides subtend.
VI.6: If two triangles have one angle equal to one angle and the sides about the equal angles proportional, the triangles is equiangular and will have those angles equal which the corresponding sides subtend.
VI.7: If two triangles have one angle equal to one angle, the sides about other angles proportional, and the remaining angles either both less or both not less than a right angle, the triangles is equiangular and will have those angles equal, the sides about which are proportional.
VI.8: If in a right-angled triangle a perpendicular be drawn from the right angle to the base, the triangles adjoining the perpendicular are similar both to the whole and to one another.
VI.9: From a given segment to cut off a prescribed part.
VI.10: Cut a given uncut segment similarly to a given cut segment.
VI.11: To two given segments to find a third proportional.
VI.12: To three given segments to find a fourth proportional.
VI.13: To two given segments to find a mean proportional.
VI.14: In equal and equiangular parallelograms the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional; and equiangular parallelograms in which the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional are equal.
VI.15: In equal triangles which have one angle equal to one angle the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional; and those triangles which have one angle equal to one angle, and in which the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional, are equal.
VI.16: If four segments be proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the rectangle contained by the means; and, if the rectangle contained by the extremes equals the rectangle contained by the means, the four segments is proportional.
VI.17: If three segments be proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the square on the mean; and, if the rectangle contained by the extremes equals the square on the mean, the three segments is proportional.
VI.18: Describe on a given segment a rectilinear figure similar and similarly situated to a given rectilinear figure.
VI.19: Similar triangles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of the corresponding sides.
VI.20: Similar polygons are divided into similar triangles, and into triangles equal in multitude and in the same ratio as the wholes, and the polygon has to the polygon a ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side has to the corresponding side.
VI.21: Figures which are similar to the same polygon are also similar to one another.
VI.22: If four segments be proportional, the polygons similar and similarly described upon them is proportional; and, if the polygons similar and similarly described upon them be proportional, the segments will themselves also be proportional.
VI.23: Equiangular parallelograms have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their sides.
VI.24: In any parallelogram the parallelograms about the diameter are similar both to the whole and to one another.
VI.25: Construct one and the same figure similar to a given polygon and equal to another given polygon.
VI.26: If from a parallelogram there be taken away a parallelogram similar and similarly situated to the whole and having a common angle with it, it is about the same diameter with the whole.
VI.27: Of all the parallelograms applied to the same segment and deficient by parallelogrammic figures similar and similarly situated to that described on the half of the segment, that parallelogram is greatest which is applied to the half of the segment and is similar to the defect.
VI.28: To a given segment to apply a parallelogram equal to a given polygon and deficient by a parallelogrammic figure similar to a given one: thus the given polygon must not be greater than the parallelogram described on the half of the segment and similar to the defect.
VI.29: To a given segment to apply a parallelogram equal to a given polygon and exceeding by a parallelogrammic figure similar to a given one.
VI.30: Cut a given segment in extreme and mean ratio.
VI.31: In right-angled triangles the figure on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the similar and similarly described figures on the sides containing the right angle.
VI.32: If two triangles having two sides proportional to two sides be placed together at one angle so that their corresponding sides are also parallel, the remaining sides of the triangles is in a segment.
VI.33: In equal circles angles have the same ratio as the arcs on which they stand, whether they stand at the centres or at the arcs.
VII.def.1: Anunit is that by virtue of which each of the things that exist is called one.
VII.def.2: Anumber is a multitude composed ofunits.
VII.def.3: Anumber is apart of a number, the less of the greater, when itmeasures the greater;
VII.def.4: Butparts when it does notmeasure it.
VII.def.5: The greaternumber is amultiple of the less when it ismeasured by the less.
VII.def.6: Aneven number is that which is divisible into two equal parts.
VII.def.7: Anodd number is that which is not divisible into two equal parts, or that which differs by anunit from aneven number.
VII.def.8: Aneven-times even number is that which ismeasured by aneven number according to an even number.
VII.def.9: Aneven-times odd number is that which ismeasured by aneven number according to anodd number.
VII.def.10: An odd-times odd number is that which is measured by an odd number according to an odd number.
VII.def.11: Aprime number is that which ismeasured by anunit alone.
VII.def.12: Numbers prime to one another are those which aremeasured by anunit alone as a common measure.
VII.def.13: Acomposite number is that which ismeasured by somenumber.
VII.def.14: Numbers composite to one another are those which aremeasured by somenumber as a common measure.
VII.def.15: Anumber is said tomultiply a number when that which is multiplied is added to itself as many times as there areunits in the other, and thus some number is produced.
VII.def.16: And, when twonumbers havingmultiplied one another make some number, the number so produced is calledplane, and itssides are the numbers which have multiplied one another.
VII.def.17: And, when threenumbers havingmultiplied one another make some number, the number so produced issolid, and itssides are the numbers which have multiplied one another.
VII.def.18: Asquare number is equalmultiplied by equal, or anumber which is contained by two equal numbers.
VII.def.19: And acube is equalmultiplied by equal and again by equal, or anumber which is contained by three equal numbers.
VII.def.20: Numbers areproportional when the first is thesame multiple, or thesame part, or thesame parts, of the second that the third is of the fourth.
VII.def.21: Similar plane and solid numbers are those which have their sidesproportional.
VII.def.22: Aperfect number is that which is equal to its own parts.
VII.1: Two unequal numbers being set out, and the less being continually subtracted in turn from the greater, if the number which is left never measures the one before it until an unit is left, the original numbers is prime to one another.
VII.2: Given two numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure.
VII.3: Given three numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure.
VII.4: Any number is either a part or parts of any number, the less of the greater.
VII.5: If a number be a part of a number, and another be the same part of another, the sum is the same part of the sum that the one is of the one.
VII.6: If a number be parts of a number, and another be the same parts of another, the sum is the same parts of the sum that the one is of the one.
VII.7: If a number be that part of a number, which a number subtracted is of a number subtracted, the remainder is the same part of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.
VII.8: If a number be the same parts of a number that a number subtracted is of a number subtracted, the remainder is the same parts of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.
VII.9: If a number be a part of a number, and another be the same part of another, alternately also, whatever part or parts the first is of the third, the same part, or the same parts, will the second also be of the fourth.
VII.10: If a number be parts of a number, and another be the same parts of another, alternately also, whatever parts or part the first is of the third, the same parts or the same part will the second also be of the fourth.
VII.11: If, as whole is to whole, so is a number subtracted to a number subtracted, the remainder is to the remainder as whole to whole.
VII.12: If there be as many numbers as we please in proportion, then, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents.
VII.13: If four numbers be proportional, they is proportional alternately.
VII.14: If there be as many numbers as we please, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio, they is in the same ratio ex aequali.
VII.15: If an unit measure any number, and another number measure any other number the same number of times, alternately also, the unit will measure the third number the same number of times that the second measures the fourth.
VII.16: If two numbers by multiplying one another make certain numbers, the numbers so produced are equal.
VII.17: If a number by multiplying two numbers make certain numbers, the numbers so produced will have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied.
VII.18: If two numbers by multiplying any number make certain numbers, the numbers so produced will have the same ratio as the multipliers.
VII.19: If four numbers be proportional, the number produced from the first and fourth will equals the number produced from the second and third; and, if the number produced from the first and fourth equals that produced from the second and third, the four numbers is proportional.
VII.20: The least numbers of those which have the same ratio with them measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the greater the greater and the less the less.
VII.21: Numbers prime to one another are the least of those which have the same ratio with them.
VII.22: The least numbers of those which have the same ratio with them are prime to one another.
VII.23: If two numbers be prime to one another, the number which measures the one of them is prime to the remaining number.
VII.24: If two numbers be prime to any number, their product also is prime to the same.
VII.25: If two numbers be prime to one another, the product of one of them into itself is prime to the remaining one.
VII.26: If two numbers be prime to two numbers, both to each, their products also is prime to one another.
VII.27: If two numbers be prime to one another, and each by multiplying itself make a certain number, the products is prime to one another; and, if the original numbers by multiplying the products make certain numbers, the latter is prime to one another [and this is always the case with the extremes].
VII.28: If two numbers be prime to one another, the sum is prime to each of them; and, if the sum of two numbers be prime to any one of them, the original numbers is prime to one another.
VII.29: Any prime number is prime to any number which it does not measure.
VII.30: If two numbers by multiplying one another make some number, and any prime number measure the product, it will also measure one of the original numbers.
VII.31: Any composite number is measured by some prime number.
VII.32: Any number either is prime or is measured by some prime number.
VII.33: Given as many numbers as we please, to find the least of those which have the same ratio with them.
VII.34: Given two numbers, to find the least number which they measure.
VII.35: If two numbers measure any number, the least number measured by them will also measure the same.
VII.36: Given three numbers, to find the least number which they measure.
VII.37: If a number be measured by any number, the number which is measured will have a part called by the same name as the measuring number.
VII.38: If a number have any part whatever, it is measured by a number called by the same name as the part.
VII.39: Find the number which is the least that will have given parts.
VIII.def.1: An unit is that by virtue of which each of the things that exist is called one.
VIII.def.2: A number is a multitude composed of units.
VIII.def.3: A number is a part of a number, the less of the greater, when it measures the greater.
VIII.def.4: but parts when it does not measure it.
VIII.def.5: The greater number is a multiple of the less when it is measured by the less.
VIII.def.6: An even number is that which is divisible into two equal parts.
VIII.def.7: An odd number is that which is not divisible into two equal parts, or that which differs by an unit from an even number.
VIII.def.8: An even-times even number is that which is measured by an even number according to an even number.
VIII.def.9: An even-times odd number is that which is measured by an even number according to an odd number.
VIII.def.10: An odd-times odd number is that which is measured by an odd number according to an odd number.
VIII.def.11: A prime number is that which is measured by an unit alone.
VIII.def.12: Numbers prime to one another are those which are measured by an unit alone as a common measure.
VIII.def.13: A composite number is that which is measured by some number.
VIII.def.14: Numbers composite to one another are those which are measured by some number as a common measure.
VIII.def.15: A number is said to multiply a number when that which is multiplied is added to itself as many times as there are units in the other, and thus some number is produced.
VIII.def.16: And, when two numbers having multiplied one another make some number, the number so produced is called plane, and its sides are the numbers which have multiplied one another.
VIII.def.17: And, when three numbers having multiplied one another make some number, the number so produced is solid, and its sides are the numbers which have multiplied one another.
VIII.def.18: A square number is equal multiplied by equal, or a number which is contained by two equal numbers.
VIII.def.19: And a cube is equal multiplied by equal and again by equal, or a number which is contained by three equal numbers.
VIII.def.20: Numbers are proportional when the first is the same multiple, or the same part, or the same parts, of the second that the third is of the fourth.
VIII.def.21: Similar plane and solid numbers are those which have their sides proportional.
VIII.def.22: A perfect number is that which is equal to its own parts.
VIII.1: If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the extremes of them be prime to one another, the numbers are the least of those which have the same ratio with them.
VIII.2: Find numbers in continued proportion, as many as may be prescribed, and the least that are in a given ratio.
VIII.3: If as many numbers as we please in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, the extremes of them are prime to one another.
VIII.4: Given as many ratios as we please in least numbers, to find numbers in continued proportion which are the least in the given ratios.
VIII.5: Plane numbers have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their sides.
VIII.6: If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the first do not measure the second, neither will any other measure any other.
VIII.7: If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the first measure the last, it will measure the second also.
VIII.8: If between two numbers there fall numbers in continued proportion with them, then, however many numbers fall between them in continued proportion, so many will also fall in continued proportion between the numbers which have the same ratio with the original numbers.
VIII.9: If two numbers be prime to one another, and numbers fall between them in continued proportion, then, however many numbers fall between them in continued proportion, so many will also fall between each of them and an unit in continued proportion.
VIII.10: If numbers fall between each of two numbers and an unit in continued proportion, however many numbers fall between each of them and an unit in continued proportion, so many also will fall between the numbers themselves in continued proportion.
VIII.11: Between two square numbers there is one mean proportional number, and the square has to the square the ratio duplicate of that which the side has to the side.
VIII.12: Between two cube numbers there are two mean proportional numbers, and the cube has to the cube the ratio triplicate of that which the side has to the side.
VIII.13: If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and each by multiplying itself make some number, the products is proportional; and, if the original numbers by multiplying the products make certain numbers, the latter is proportional.
VIII.14: If a square measure a square, the side will also measure the side; and, if the side measure the side, the square will also measure the square.
VIII.15: If a cube number measure a cube number, the side will also measure the side; and, if the side measure the side, the cube will also measure the cube.
VIII.16: If a square number do not measure a square number, neither will the side measure the side; and, if the side do not measure the side, neither will the square measure the square.
VIII.17: If a cube number do not measure a cube number, neither will the side measure the side; and, if the side do not measure the side, neither will the cube measure the cube.
VIII.18: Between two similar plane numbers there is one mean proportional number; and the plane number has to the plane number the ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side has to the corresponding side.
VIII.19: Between two similar solid numbers there fall two mean proportional numbers; and the solid number has to the similar solid number the ratio triplicate of that which the corresponding side has to the corresponding side.
VIII.20: If one mean proportional number fall between two numbers, the numbers is similar plane numbers.
VIII.21: If two mean proportional numbers fall between two numbers, the numbers are similar solid numbers.
VIII.22: If three numbers be in continued proportion, and the first be square, the third is square.
VIII.23: If four numbers be in continued proportion, and the first be cube, the fourth is cube.
VIII.24: If two numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and the first be square, the second is square.
VIII.25: If two numbers have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number, and the first be cube, the second is cube.
VIII.26: Similar plane numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.
VIII.27: Similar solid numbers have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number.
IX.1: If two similar plane numbers by multiplying one another make some number, the product is square.
IX.2: If two numbers by multiplying one another make a square number, they are similar plane numbers.
IX.3: If a cube number by multiplying itself make some number, the product is cube.
IX.4: If a cube number by multiplying a cube number make some number, the product is cube.
IX.5: If a cube number by multiplying any number make a cube number, the multiplied number is cube.
IX.6: If a number by multiplying itself make a cube number, it will itself also be cube.
IX.7: If a composite number by multiplying any number make some number, the product is solid.
IX.8: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the third from the unit is square, as will also those which successively leave out one; the fourth is cube, as will also all those which leave out two; and the seventh is at once cube and square, as will also those which leave out five.
IX.9: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be square, all the rest is square. And, if the number after the unit be cube, all the rest is cube.
IX.10: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be not square, neither will any other be square except the third from the unit and all those which leave out one. And, if the number after the unit be not cube, neither will any other be cube except the fourth from the unit and all those which leave out two.
IX.11: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the less measures the greater according to some one of the numbers which have place among the proportional numbers.
IX.12: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit is measured by the same.
IX.13: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be prime, the greatest will not be measured by any except those which have a place among the proportional numbers.
IX.14: If a number be the least that is measured by prime numbers, it will not be measured by any other prime number except those originally measuring it.
IX.15: If three numbers in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, any two whatever added together is prime to the remaining number.
IX.16: If two numbers be prime to one another, the second will not be to any other number as the first is to the second.
IX.17: If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the extremes of them be prime to one another, the last will not be to any other number as the first to the second.
IX.18: Given two numbers, to investigate whether it is possible to find a third proportional to them.
IX.19: Given three numbers, to investigate when it is possible to find a fourth proportional to them.
IX.20: Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.
IX.21: If as many even numbers as we please be added together, the whole is even.
IX.22: If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be even, the whole is even.
IX.23: If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be odd, the whole is odd.
IX.24: If from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder is even.
IX.25: If from an even number an odd number be subtracted, the remainder is odd.
IX.26: If from an odd number an odd number be subtracted, the remainder is even.
IX.27: If from an odd number an even number be subtracted, the remainder is odd.
IX.28: If an odd number by multiplying an even number make some number, the product is even.
IX.29: If an odd number by multiplying an odd number make some number, the product is odd.
IX.30: If an odd number measure an even number, it will also measure the half of it.
IX.31: If an odd number be prime to any number, it is prime to the double of it.
IX.32: Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.
IX.33: If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.
IX.34: If a number neither be one of those which are continually doubled from a dyad, nor have its half odd, it is both even-times even and even-times odd.
IX.35: If as many numbers as we please be in continued proportion, and there be subtracted from the second and the last numbers equal to the first, then, as the excess of the second is to the first, so will the excess of the last be to all those before it.
IX.36: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be set out continuously in double proportion, until the sum of all becomes prime, and if the sum multiplied into the last make some number, the product is perfect.
