X.def.2: Straight lines arecommensurable in square when thesquares on them aremeasured by the same area, andincommensurable in square when the squares on them cannot possibly have any area as a common measure.
X.def.3: With these hypotheses, it is proved that there existsegments infinite in multitude which arecommensurable and incommensurable respectively, some in length only, and others in square also, with an assigned segment. Let then the assigned segment be calledrational, and those segments which are commensurable with it, whether in length and in square or in square only,rational, but those which are incommensurable with itirrational.
X.def.4: And let thesquare on the assignedsegment be calledrational and those areas which arecommensurable with itrational, but those which are incommensurable with itirrational, and the segments which produce themirrational, that is, in case the areas are squares, the sides themselves, but in case they are any otherpolygons, the segments on which are described squares equal to them.
X.def.ii.1: Given arationalsegment and a binomial, divided into its terms, such that thesquare on the greater term is greater than the square on the lesser by the square on a segmentcommensurable in length with the greater, then, if the greater term be commensurable in length with the rational segment set out, let the whole be called afirst binomial segment;
X.def.ii.2: But if the lesser term becommensurable in length with therationalsegment set out, let the whole be called asecond binomial;
X.def.ii.3: And if neither of the terms becommensurable in length with therationalsegment set out, let the whole be called athird binomial.
X.def.ii.4: Again, if thesquare on the greater term be greater than the square on the lesser by the square on asegment incommensurable in length with the greater, then, if the greater term becommensurable in length with therational segment set out, let the whole be called afourth binomial;
X.def.iii.1: Given arationalsegment and an apotome, if thesquare on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a segmentcommensurable in length with the whole, and the whole be commensurable in length with the rational segment set out, let the apotome be called afirst apotome.
X.def.iii.2: But if the annex becommensurable in length with therationalsegment set out, and thesquare on the whole be greater than that on the annex by the square on a segment commensurable with the whole, let the apotome be called asecond apotome.
X.def.iii.3: But if neither becommensurable in length with therationalsegment set out, and thesquare on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a segment commensurable with the whole, let the apotome be called athird apotome.
X.def.iii.4: Again, if thesquare on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on asegment incommensurable with the whole, then, if the whole becommensurable in length with therational segment set out, let the apotome be called afourth apotome;
X.def.iii.5: If the annex be socommensurable, afifth;
X.1: Two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there be subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process be repeated continually, there is left some magnitude which is less than the lesser magnitude set out.
X.2: If, when the less of two unequal magnitudes is continually subtracted in turn from the greater, that which is left never measures the one before it, the magnitudes is incommensurable.
X.3: Given two commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.
X.4: Given three commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.
X.5: Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
X.6: If two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes is commensurable.
X.7: Incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
X.8: If two magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes is incommensurable.
X.9: The squares on segments commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length. But the squares on segments incommensurable in length have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will not have their sides commensurable in length either.
X.10: Find two segments incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with an assigned segment.
X.11: If four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be commensurable with the second, the third is commensurable with the fourth; and, if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third is incommensurable with the fourth.
X.12: Magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another also.
X.13: If two magnitudes be commensurable, and the one of them be incommensurable with any magnitude, the remaining one is incommensurable with the same.
X.14: If four segments be proportional, and the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a segment commensurable with the first, the square on the third is greater than the square on the fourth by the square on a segment commensurable with the third. And, if the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a segment incommensurable with the first, the square on the third is greater than the square on the fourth by the square on a segment incommensurable with the third.
X.15: If two commensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole is commensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be commensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes is commensurable.
X.16: If two incommensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole is incommensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be incommensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes is incommensurable.
X.17: If there be two unequal segments, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are commensurable in length, then the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment commensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment commensurable with the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it will divide it into parts which are commensurable in length.
X.18: If there be two unequal segments, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are incommensurable, the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment incommensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment incommensurable with the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into parts which are incommensurable.
X.19: The rectangle contained by rational segments commensurable in length is rational.
X.20: If a rational area be applied to a rational segment, it produces as breadth a segment rational and commensurable in length with the segment to which it is applied.
X.21: The rectangle contained by rational segments commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial.
X.22: The square on a medial segment, if applied to a rational segment, produces as breadth a segment rational and incommensurable in length with that to which it is applied.
X.23: A segment commensurable with a medial segment is medial.
X.24: The rectangle contained by medial segments commensurable in length is medial.
X.25: The rectangle contained by medial segments commensurable in square only is either rational or medial.
X.26: A medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area.
X.27: Find medial segments commensurable in square only which contain a rational rectangle.
X.28: Find medial segments commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle.
X.29: Find two rational segments commensurable in square only and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment commensurable in length with the greater.
X.30: Find two rational segments commensurable in square only and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment incommensurable in length with the greater.
X.31: Find two medial segments commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment commensurable in length with the greater.
X.32: Find two medial segments commensurable in square only, containing a medial rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a segment commensurable with the greater.
X.33: Find two segments incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial.
X.34: Find two segments incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial but the rectangle contained by them rational.
X.35: Find two segments incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial and the rectangle contained by them medial and moreover incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
X.36: If two rational segments commensurable in square only be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called binomial.
X.37: If two medial segments commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called a first bimedial segment.
X.38: If two medial segments commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called a second bimedial segment.
X.39: If two segments incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational, but the rectangle contained by them medial, be added together, the whole segment is irrational: and let it be called major.
X.40: If two segments incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, but the rectangle contained by them rational, be added together, the whole segment is irrational; and let it be called the side of a rational plus a medial area.
X.41: If two segments incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, and the rectangle contained by them medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them, be added together, the whole segment is irrational; and let it be called the side of the sum of two medial areas.
X.42: A binomial segment is divided into its terms at one point only.
X.43: A first bimedial segment is divided at one point only.
X.44: A second bimedial segment is divided at one point only.
X.45: A major segment is divided at one and the same point only.
X.46: The side of a rational plus a medial area is divided at one point only.
X.47: The side of the sum of two medial areas is divided at one point only.
X.54: If an area be contained by a rational segment and the first binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational segment which is called binomial.
X.55: If an area be contained by a rational segment and the second binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational segment which is called a first bimedial.
X.56: If an area be contained by a rational segment and the third binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational segment called a second bimedial.
X.57: If an area be contained by a rational segment and the fourth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational segment called major.
X.58: If an area be contained by a rational segment and the fifth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational segment called the side of a rational plus a medial area.
X.59: If an area be contained by a rational segment and the sixth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational segment called the side of the sum of two medial areas.
X.60: The square on the binomial segment applied to a rational segment produces as breadth the first binomial.
X.61: The square on the first bimedial segment applied to a rational segment produces as breadth the second binomial.
X.62: The square on the second bimedial segment applied to a rational segment produces as breadth the third binomial.
X.63: The square on the major segment applied to a rational segment produces as breadth the fourth binomial.
X.64: The square on the side of a rational plus a medial area applied to a rational segment produces as breadth the fifth binomial.
X.65: The square on the side of the sum of two medial areas applied to a rational segment produces as breadth the sixth binomial.
X.66: A segment commensurable in length with a binomial segment is itself also binomial and the same in order.
X.67: A segment commensurable in length with a bimedial segment is itself also bimedial and the same in order.
X.68: A segment commensurable with a major segment is itself also major.
X.69: A segment commensurable with the side of a rational plus a medial area is itself also the side of a rational plus a medial area.
X.70: A segment commensurable with the side of the sum of two medial areas is the side of the sum of two medial areas.
X.71: If a rational and a medial area be added together, four irrational segments arise, namely a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area.
X.72: If two medial areas incommensurable with one another be added together, the remaining two irrational segments arise, namely either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.
X.73: If from a rational segment there be subtracted a rational segment commensurable with the whole in square only, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called an apotome.
X.74: If from a medial segment there be subtracted a medial segment which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle, the remainder is irrational. And let it be called a first apotome of a medial segment.
X.75: If from a medial segment there be subtracted a medial segment which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called a second apotome of a medial segment.
X.76: If from a segment there be subtracted a segment which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the squares on them added together rational, but the rectangle contained by them medial, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called minor.
X.77: If from a segment there be subtracted a segment which is incommensurable in square with the whole, and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational, the remainder is irrational: and let it be called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
X.78: If from a segment there be subtracted a segment which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial, twice the rectangle contained by them medial, and further the squares on them incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called that which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
X.79: To an apotome only one rational segment can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only.
X.80: To a first apotome of a medial segment only one medial segment can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle.
X.81: To a second apotome of a medial segment only one medial segment can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle.
X.82: To a minor segment only one segment can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which makes, with the whole, the sum of the squares on them rational but twice the rectangle contained by them medial.
X.83: To a segment which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one segment can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole segment and which with the whole segment makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.
X.84: To a segment which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one segment can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole segment and which with the whole segment makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
X.91: If an area be contained by a rational segment and a first apotome, the "side" of the area is an apotome.
X.92: If an area be contained by a rational segment and a second apotome, the "side" of the area is a first apotome of a medial segment.
X.93: If an area be contained by a rational segment and a third apotome, the “side” of the area is a second apotome of a medial segment.
X.94: If an area be contained by a rational segment and a fourth apotome, the “side” of the area is minor.
X.95: If an area be contained by a rational segment and a fifth apotome, the “side” of the area is a segment which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
X.96: If an area be contained by a rational segment and a sixth apotome, the “side” of the area is a segment which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
X.97: The square on an apotome applied to a rational segment produces as breadth a first apotome.
X.98: The square on a first apotome of a medial segment applied to a rational segment produces as breadth a second apotome.
X.99: The square on a second apotome of a medial segment applied to a rational segment produces as breadth a third apotome.
X.100: The square on a minor segment applied to a rational segment produces as breadth a fourth apotome.
X.101: The square on the segment which produces with a rational area a medial whole, if applied to a rational segment, produces as breadth a fifth apotome.
X.102: The square on the segment which produces with a medial area a medial whole, if applied to a rational segment, produces as breadth a sixth apotome.
X.103: A segment commensurable in length with an apotome is an apotome and the same in order.
X.104: A segment commensurable with an apotome of a medial segment is an apotome of a medial segment and the same in order.
X.105: A segment commensurable with a minor segment is minor.
X.106: A segment commensurable with that which produces with a rational area a medial whole is a segment which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
X.107: A segment commensurable with that which produces with a medial area a medial whole is itself also a segment which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
X.108: If from a rational area a medial area be subtracted, the “side” of the remaining area becomes one of two irrational segments, either an apotome or a minor segment.
X.109: If from a medial area a rational area be subtracted, there arise two other irrational segments, either a first apotome of a medial segment or a segment which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
X.110: If from a medial area there be subtracted a medial area incommensurable with the whole, the two remaining irrational segments arise, either a second apotome of a medial segment or a segment which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
X.111: The apotome is not the same with the binomial segment.
X.112: The square on a rational segment applied to the binomial segment produces as breadth an apotome the terms of which are commensurable with the terms of the binomial and moreover in the same ratio; and further the apotome so arising will have the same order as the binomial segment.
X.113: The square on a rational segment, if applied to an apotome, produces as breadth the binomial segment the terms of which are commensurable with the terms of the apotome and in the same ratio; and further the binomial so arising has the same order as the apotome.
X.114: If an area be contained by an apotome and the binomial segment the terms of which are commensurable with the terms of the apotome and in the same ratio, the “side” of the area is rational.
X.115: From a medial segment there arise irrational segments infinite in number, and none of them is the same as any of the preceding.
XI.def.1: Asolid is that which has length, breadth, and depth.
XI.def.3: Asegment isat right angles to a plane, when it makesright angles with all the segments which meet it and are in theplane.
XI.def.4: Aplane is at right angles to a plane when thesegments drawn, in one of theplanes,at right angles to the common section of the planes are at right angles to the remaining plane.
XI.def.5: The inclination of a straight line to a plane is, assuming a perpendicular drawn from the extremity of the straight line which is elevated above the plane to the plane, and a straight line joined from the point thus arising to the extremity of the straight line which is in the plane, the angle contained by the straight line so drawn and the straight line standing up.
XI.def.6: The inclination of a plane to a plane is the acute angle contained by the straight lines drawn at right angles to the common section at the same point, one in each of the planes.
XI.def.7: A plane is said to be similarly inclined to a plane as another is to another when the said angles of the inclinations are equal to one another.
XI.def.8: Parallel planes are those which do not meet.
XI.def.9: Similar solid figures are thosecontained by similar planes equal in multitude.
XI.def.10: Equal and similar solid figures are thosecontained by similar planes equal in multitude and in magnitude.
XI.def.11: Asolid angle is the inclination constituted by more than twolines which meet one another and are not in the samesurface, towards all the lines. Otherwise: Asolid angle is that which is contained by more than twoplane angles which are not in the sameplane and are constructed to onepoint.
XI.def.12: Apyramid is asolid figure, contained byplanes, which is constructed from one plane to onepoint.
XI.def.13: Aprism is asolid figure contained byplanes two of which, namely those which are opposite, are equal, similar andparallel, while the rest are parallelograms.
XI.def.14: When, thediameter of asemicircle remaining fixed, the semicircle is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, thefigure so comprehended is asphere.
XI.def.15: Theaxis of the sphere is thesegment which remains fixed and about which thesemicircle is turned.
XI.def.16: Thecenter of the sphere is the same as that of thesemicircle.
XI.def.17: Adiameter of the sphere is anysegment drawn through thecenter and terminated in both directions by thesurface of thesphere.
XI.def.18: When, one side of those about theright angle in aright-angled triangle remaining fixed, thetriangle is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, thefigure so comprehended is acone. And, if thesegment which remains fixed equals the remaining side about the right angle which is carried round, the cone isright-angled; if less,obtuse-angled; and if greater,acute-angled.
XI.def.19: Theaxis of the cone is thesegment which remains fixed and about which thetriangle is turned.
XI.def.20: And thebase is thecircle described by thesegment which is carried round.
XI.def.21: When, one side of those about theright angle in arectangular parallelogram remaining fixed, the parallelogram is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, thefigure so comprehended is acylinder.
XI.def.22: Theaxis of the cylinder is thesegment which remains fixed and about which the parallelogram is turned.
XI.def.23: And thebases are thecircles described by the two sides opposite to one another which are carried round.
XI.def.24: Similar cones and cylinders are those in which theaxes and thediameters of the bases areproportional.
XI.def.25: Acube is asolid figure contained by six equalsquares.
XI.def.26: Anoctahedron is asolid figure contained by eight equal andequilateral triangles.
XI.def.27: Anicosahedron is asolid figure contained by twenty equal andequilateral triangles.
XI.def.28: Adodecahedron is asolid figure contained by twelve equal,equilateral, and equiangular pentagons.
XI.1: A part of a segment cannot be in the plane of reference and a part in a plane more elevated.
XI.2: If two segments cut one another, they are in one plane, and every triangle is in one plane.
XI.3: If two planes cut one another, their common section is a segment.
XI.4: If a segment be set up at right angles to two segments which cut one another, at their common point of section, it is at right angles to the plane through them.
XI.5: If a segment be set up at right angles to three segments which meet one another, at their common point of section, the three segments are in one plane.
XI.6: If two segments be at right angles to the same plane, the segments is parallel.
XI.7: If two segments be parallel and points be taken at random on each of them, the segment joining the points is in the same plane with the parallel lines.
XI.8: If two segments be parallel, and one of them be at right angles to any plane, the remaining one is at right angles to the same plane.
XI.9: Straight lines which are parallel to the same segment and are not in the same plane with it are also parallel to one another.
XI.10: If two segments meeting one another be parallel to two segments meeting one another not in the same plane, they will contain equal angles.
XI.11: From a given elevated point to draw a segment perpendicular to a given plane.
XI.12: To set up a segment at right angles to a given plane from a given point in it.
XI.13: From the same point two segments cannot be set up at right angles to the same plane on the same side.
XI.14: Planes to which the same segment is at right angles is parallel.
XI.15: If two segments meeting one another be parallel to two segments meeting one another, not being in the same plane, the planes through them are parallel.
XI.16: If two parallel planes be cut by any plane, their common sections are parallel.
XI.17: If two segments be cut by parallel planes, they is cut in the same ratios.
XI.18: If a segment be at right angles to any plane, all the planes through it is at right angles to the same plane.
XI.19: If two planes which cut one another be at right angles to any plane, their common section is at right angles to the same plane.
XI.20: If a solid angle be contained by three plane angles, any two, taken together in any manner, are greater than the remaining one.
XI.21: Any solid angle is contained by plane angles less than four right angles.
XI.22: If there be three plane angles of which two, taken together in any manner, are greater than the remaining one, and they are contained by equal segments, it is possible to construct a triangle out of the segments joining the extremities of the equal segments.
XI.23: Construct a solid angle out of three plane angles two of which, taken together in any manner, are greater than the remaining one: thus the three angles must be less than four right angles.
XI.24: If a solid be contained by parallel planes, the opposite planes in it are equal and parallelogrammic.
XI.25: If a parallelepipedal solid be cut by a plane which is parallel to the opposite planes, then, as the base is to the base, so will the solid be to the solid.
XI.26: On a given segment, and at a given point on it, to construct a solid angle equal to a given solid angle.
XI.27: Describe on a given segment a parallelepipedal solid similar and similarly situated to a given parallelepipedal solid.
XI.28: If a parallelepipedal solid be cut by a plane through the diagonals of the opposite planes, the solid is bisected by the plane.
XI.29: Parallelepipedal solids which are on the same base and of the same height, and in which the extremities of the sides which stand up are on the same segments, are equal.
XI.30: Parallelepipedal solids which are on the same base and of the same height, and in which the extremities of the sides which stand up are not on the same segments, are equal.
XI.31: Parallelepipedal solids which are on equal bases and of the same height are equal.
XI.32: Parallelepipedal solids which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.
XI.33: Similar parallelepipedal solids are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.
XI.34: In equal parallelepipedal solids the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those parallelepipedal solids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.
XI.35: If there be two equal plane angles, and on their vertices there be set up elevated segments containing equal angles with the original segments respectively, if on the elevated segments points be taken at random and perpendiculars be drawn from them to the planes in which the original angles are, and if from the points so arising in the planes segments be joined to the vertices of the original angles, they will contain, with the elevated segments, equal angles.
XI.36: If three segments be proportional, the parallelepipedal solid formed out of the three is equal to the parallelepipedal solid on the mean which is equilateral, but equiangular with the aforesaid solid.
XI.37: If four segments be proportional, the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described is proportional; and, if the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described be proportional, the segments will themselves also be proportional.
XI.38: If the sides of the opposite planes of a cube be bisected, and planes be carried through the points of section, the common section of the planes and the diameter of the cube bisect one another.
XI.39: If there be two prisms of equal height, and one have a parallelogram as base and the other a triangle, and if the parallelogram be double of the triangle, the prisms is equal.
XII.1: Similar polygons inscribed in circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters.
XII.2: Circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters.
XII.3: Any pyramid which has a triangular base is divided into two pyramids equal and similar to one another, similar to the whole and having triangular bases, and into two equal prisms; and the two prisms are greater than the half of the whole pyramid.
XII.4: If there be two pyramids of the same height which have triangular bases, and each of them be divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, then, as the base of the one pyramid is to the base of the other pyramid, so will all the prisms in the one pyramid be to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the other pyramid.
XII.5: Pyramids which are of the same height and have triangular bases are to one another as the bases.
XII.6: Pyramids which are of the same height and have polygonal bases are to one another as the bases.
XII.7: Any prism which has a triangular base is divided into three pyramids equal to one another which have triangular bases.
XII.8: Similar pyramids which have triangular bases are in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.
XII.9: In equal pyramids which have triangular bases the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those pyramids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.
XII.10: Any cone is a third part of the cylinder which has the same base with it and equal height.
XII.11: Cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.
XII.12: Similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases.
XII.13: If a cylinder be cut by a plane which is parallel to its opposite planes, then, as the cylinder is to the cylinder, so will the axis be to the axis.
XII.14: Cones and cylinders which are on equal bases are to one another as their heights.
XII.15: In equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.
XII.16: Given two circles about the same center, to inscribe in the greater circle an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle.
XII.17: Given two spheres about the same center, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.
XII.18: Spheres are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their respective diameters.
XIII.1: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the greater segment added to the half of the whole is five times the square on the half.
XIII.2: If the square on a segment be five times the square on a segment of it, then, when the double of the said segment is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the remaining part of the original segment.
XIII.3: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the lesser segment added to the half of the greater segment is five times the square on the half of the greater segment.
XIII.4: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the whole and the square on the lesser segment together are triple of the square on the greater segment.
XIII.5: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, and there be added to it a segment equal to the greater segment, the whole segment has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the original segment is the greater segment.
XIII.6: If a rational segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, each of the segments is the irrational segment called apotome.
XIII.7: If three angles of an equilateral pentagon, taken either in order or not in order, be equal, the pentagon is equiangular.
XIII.8: If in an equilateral and equiangular pentagon segments subtend two angles taken in order, they cut one another in extreme and mean ratio, and their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon.
XIII.9: If the side of the hexagon and that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle be added together, the whole segment has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and its greater segment is the side of the hexagon.
XIII.10: If an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle.
XIII.11: If in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational segment called minor.
XIII.12: If an equilateral triangle be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the triangle is triple of the square on the radius of the circle.
XIII.13: To construct a pyramid, to comprehend it in a given sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid.
XIII.14: Construct an octahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, as in the preceding case; and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is double of the square on the side of the octahedron.
XIII.15: Construct a cube and comprehend it in a sphere, like the pyramid; and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube.
XIII.16: Construct an icosahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures; and to prove that the side of the icosahedron is the irrational segment called minor.
XIII.17: Construct a dodecahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational segment called apotome.
XIII.18: To set out the sides of the five figures and to compare them with one another.

G.23: Things / A B /, / D E / that coincide with one another are equal to one another.
G.24: Triangles with two sides and the included angle equal are congruent (SAS).
G.25: In an isosceles triangle, the angles at the base are equal, and if the equal sides are extended, the angles under the base are equal.

G.27: If two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides subtending the equal angles are also equal.

G.30: A rectilineal angle is contained by two segments or lines.

G.34: Construct a segment at right angles to a given line from a given point on it.
G.35: Construct a perpendicular to a given line from a given point not on it.
G.36: If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
G.37: A segment standing on a line makes either two right angles or adjacent angles summing to two right angles.
G.39: If two segments at a point on a line on opposite sides make adjacent angles summing to two right angles, the two segments are collinear.
G.40: Intersecting lines make their vertical angles equal.
G.41: In any triangle, if one side is extended, the exterior angle is greater than either opposite interior angle.
G.42: In any triangle, the sum of any two angles is less than two right angles.
G.43: In any triangle, the greater side subtends the greater angle.
G.44: In any triangle, the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.
G.45: In any triangle, the sum of any two sides is greater than the remaining side.
G.46: Segments constructed from the endpoints of one side of a triangle to an interior point have a lesser sum but contain a greater angle than the other two sides.
G.47: Construct a triangle from three segments equal to three given segments satisfying the triangle inequality.
G.48: Construct on a given line at a given point an angle equal to a given angle.
G.49: If two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively, the one with the greater included angle has the greater base.
G.50: If two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively, the one with the greater base has the greater included angle.
G.51: Triangles with two angles and one corresponding side equal are congruent (ASA / AAS).
G.52: Parallel lines are lines in the same plane which, extended indefinitely in both directions, do not meet.
G.53: If a transversal cutting two lines makes the alternate interior angles equal, the lines are parallel.
G.54: If a transversal cutting two lines makes the exterior angle equal to the opposite interior angle, or interior angles on the same side supplementary, the lines are parallel.
G.55: Two lines intersected by a transversal with interior angles on one side summing to less than two right angles meet on that side.
G.56: A transversal cutting parallel lines makes alternate interior angles equal, exterior and opposite interior angles equal, and same-side interior angles supplementary.
G.57: Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to one another.
G.58: Construct through a given point a line parallel to a given line.
G.59: In any triangle, an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, and the three interior angles sum to two right angles.
G.60: Segments joining the endpoints of equal and parallel segments in the same directions are themselves equal and parallel.
G.61: A diameter of a circle is any segment drawn through the center and terminated in both directions by the arc of the circle; it bisects the circle.
G.62: In a parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, and the diagonal bisects the area.
G.63: Of quadrilateral figures, a square is equilateral and right-angled; an oblong is right-angled but not equilateral; a rhombus is equilateral but not right-angled; a rhomboid has opposite sides and angles equal but is neither equilateral nor right-angled.
G.64: Parallelograms on the same base and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.65: Parallelograms on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.66: Triangles on the same base and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.67: Triangles on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal in area.
G.68: Equal triangles on the same base and on the same side lie in the same parallels.
G.69: Equal triangles on equal bases and on the same side lie in the same parallels.
G.70: If a parallelogram shares the same base with a triangle and lies in the same parallels, the parallelogram is double the triangle.
G.71: Construct, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given triangle.
G.72: In any parallelogram, the complements of the parallelograms about the diagonal are equal in area.
G.73: Apply to a given segment, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given triangle.
G.74: Construct, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal in area to a given polygon.
G.75: Construct a square on a given segment.
G.76: An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle.
G.77: An acute angle is less than a right angle.
G.78: A right-angled triangle has a right angle, an obtuse-angled triangle has an obtuse angle, and an acute-angled triangle has three acute angles.
G.79: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the two legs (Pythagorean Theorem).

G.538: If a parallelepipedal solid be cut by a plane through the diagonals of the opposite planes, the solid is bisected by the plane.

G.547: If four segments be proportional, the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described is proportional; and, if the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described be proportional, the segments will themselves also be proportional.
G.548: Acube is asolid figure contained by six equalsquares.

G.552: Circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters.

G.556: Pyramids which are of the same height and have triangular bases are to one another as the bases.
G.557: Pyramids which are of the same height and have polygonal bases are to one another as the bases.
G.558: Any prism which has a triangular base is divided into three pyramids equal to one another which have triangular bases.

G.560: In equal pyramids which have triangular bases the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those pyramids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

G.569: Similar cones and cylinders are those in which theaxes and thediameters of the bases areproportional.
G.570: Similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases.
G.571: If a cylinder be cut by a plane which is parallel to its opposite planes, then, as the cylinder is to the cylinder, so will the axis be to the axis.
G.572: Cones and cylinders which are on equal bases are to one another as their heights.
G.573: In equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.
G.574: Given two circles about the same center, to inscribe in the greater circle an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle.
G.575: When, thediameter of asemicircle remaining fixed, the semicircle is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, thefigure so comprehended is asphere.
G.576: Adiameter of the sphere is anysegment drawn through thecenter and terminated in both directions by thesurface of thesphere.
G.577: Given two spheres about the same center, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.
G.578: Spheres are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their respective diameters.
G.579: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the greater segment added to the half of the whole is five times the square on the half.
G.580: If the square on a segment be five times the square on a segment of it, then, when the double of the said segment is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the remaining part of the original segment.
G.581: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the lesser segment added to the half of the greater segment is five times the square on the half of the greater segment.
G.582: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the whole and the square on the lesser segment together are triple of the square on the greater segment.
G.583: If a segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, and there be added to it a segment equal to the greater segment, the whole segment has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the original segment is the greater segment.
G.584: If a rational segment be cut in extreme and mean ratio, each of the segments is the irrational segment called apotome.
G.585: If three angles of an equilateral pentagon, taken either in order or not in order, be equal, the pentagon is equiangular.

G.588: If an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle.
G.589: If in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational segment called minor.
G.590: If an equilateral triangle be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the triangle is triple of the square on the radius of the circle.
